research_request.role: You are a senior networking researcher who supervises MTech and PhD students. Help two third-year B.Tech CSE students frame a defensible research problem for a semester project. Be critical and specific. Prefer depth to breadth. Never invent citations.

project_context.course: CS301 Computer Networks, NIT Karnataka Surathkal, Semester V (Oct 2026)
project_context.guide: Prof. B. R. Chandavarkar, Dept. of CSE, NITK. He examines by application and expects rigorous networking content. His published research areas are worth checking (we believe they include underwater acoustic networks, which is relevant to UnetStack; verify this).
project_context.audience_for_defense: MTech and PhD students who will attack novelty, assumptions, evaluation validity and tool choice.
project_context.deliverables: A progress-report-style paper (LaTeX, IEEE-style references), an implementation, and an oral defense.
project_context.hard_constraint: The implementation and evaluation MUST use exactly one of: UnetStack, ns-3, or MATLAB. No other emulator or simulator is allowed.
project_context.team_background: Last semester we built application-layer packet FEC (GF(256) Cauchy codes) for 5G URLLC in Python, with Bernoulli, Gilbert-Elliott and MATLAB 5G Toolbox nrTDLChannel channel models. So we are comfortable with MATLAB, Python, loss models and Wireshark. We have not used ns-3 or UnetStack before.

base_paper.citation: R. Nakamura and N. Kamiyama, "Analysis of Similarity Caching on General Cache Networks," IEEE Access, vol. 12, pp. 163338-163348, 2024, doi:10.1109/ACCESS.2024.3489620.
base_paper.model: Cache network G=(V,E) with cache nodes (capacity B) and origin nodes. A request for content c travels a fixed path toward the origin (CCN/NDN request-response). At each cache, with probability alpha, the node returns its most similar cached item argmax s(c,c'); otherwise it forwards. The origin returns c exactly. The client accepts if s(c,c') >= its threshold s; otherwise it waits delta and re-requests. The metric is "similar-content delivery delay": D = sum_s beta(s) * D^{s(>=)}, where D^{s(>=)} = sum_n Delta_n R_n, Delta_n = (n-1)(d^{s(<)} + delta) + d^{s(>=)}, and R_n = (1-rho)^(n-1) rho. Cache contents are modelled as a uniform random B-subset (combinatorial Eq. 3).
base_paper.evaluation: Numerical only. A tandem of 5 caches plus 1 origin, 1 ms links, B=10, delta=10 ms, uniform popularity. Datasets: synthetic similarity from |a-b|^gamma (C=100) and 788 Kaggle motorbike images (ORB features).
base_paper.their_findings: Delay rises with the required similarity. Large alpha helps low-similarity users and hurts high-similarity users. Client position (distance to origin) matters, and fairness across clients depends on alpha.
base_paper.their_future_work: Other topologies; a concrete network architecture; a smarter client that fetches higher-similarity content instead of blindly retrying.

our_verified_findings.finding: Eq. (6) as printed weights only the last-hop RTT by the probability that node i serves. Expected delay needs the cumulative RTT. Their Fig. 5(a) matches the cumulative version: we reproduced s=1 values of 9.96 / 45.97 / 80.6 ms for alpha = 0.1 / 0.5 / 0.9, against roughly 10 / 50 / 87 in the paper. So it is a typographical error.

Eq. (8) lets a request pass a node that served an unacceptable item, which implies a threshold-aware cache. Eq. (10) stops the request whenever a node answers, which implies a blind cache. The delay terms and the retry probability therefore appear to model different systems.

The model treats retries as independent draws of cache contents. Real caches keep their contents across a 10 ms retry. With persistent contents, on the paper's own setup, mean delay is underestimated by about 2x at alpha=0.5 and by 64x-1700x at alpha=0.9. At alpha=0.9 and s=1, P(delay > 1 s) = 0.65 and the worst case is about 1000 s, because (1-alpha)^5 = 1e-5. The cause is Jensen's inequality: E[1/rho] >= 1/E[rho]. Caveat: churn from other users' requests sits between the two extremes.

candidate_directions.note: Our current shortlist. Challenge it, merge it, or replace it.
candidate_directions.ps: Threshold-carrying requests (s_min in the request) and bounded-retry variants (exclusion bitmap, hop escalation). Under threshold-aware requests, alpha=1 is delay-optimal.

Congestion- and loss-aware similarity caching. Add queueing and burst loss (Gilbert-Elliott) to the model. Approximation acts as a congestion valve. Hypothesis: a good AQM reduces the optimal amount of approximation.

A per-node, delay-optimal answer/forward rule: answer iff s' >= F^-1(1 - D_up / (delta + D_retry)). D_up is learned with TCP-style SRTT estimation; F (the user acceptance CDF) is learned from retries as implicit NACKs. Our current favourite.
LSH-in-Bloom-filter digests for off-path cooperative similarity lookup on general topologies.
Privacy: timing and content leakage in similarity cache networks, with alpha as a randomised-response knob.
Hubness-based cache pollution and a rejection-feedback defense.
DASH representation substitution: serve a cached different bitrate as the "similar" item.
Tiered semantic caching for LLM queries, allocating an error budget across network tiers (Quora Question Pairs labels as ground truth). Closest prior work: arXiv 2602.13165.

tasks.task: Survey active research on similarity, approximate and semantic caching: cache networks, ICN/NDN, edge/MEC, LLM semantic caching, computation reuse, and security or privacy of approximate caches. Include work on caching or ICN in UNDERWATER acoustic networks and DTNs, and in vehicular or satellite networks (long-delay, lossy links, where similarity caching may matter most). For each paper give: full citation with DOI or arXiv ID, two lines on what it does, and the precise gap it leaves.

Assess whether similarity caching makes MORE sense in underwater acoustic networks. Consider: ~1500 m/s propagation (seconds-scale RTT), kbps links, high loss, energy-limited nodes, and sensor data that is naturally similar in space and time. Then: how the base paper's delay model changes when tau is seconds and delta is comparable to the RTT; what "similarity" means for sensor or AUV data; and whether there is published work on approximate or semantic caching underwater. Propose 2-3 problem statements specific to this setting if it is promising.

Critically re-check our findings F1-F3. Is any of them wrong, already known in the literature, or weaker than we think? Then rank the problem statements on: novelty, networking depth (fit for a networks professor), tool fit, theory content, implementation effort, and defense strength.

rules.rule: Cite only papers you are confident exist. Give DOI or arXiv ID. Mark anything uncertain as [UNVERIFIED]. A wrong citation is worse than a missing one.
Separate facts (from papers or documentation) from your own reasoning or speculation. Label speculation.
Be concrete: name equations, parameters, APIs, modules and metrics. Avoid generic advice such as "use machine learning" or "consider scalability".
Scope for a one-semester, two-person project. Flag anything that would not fit.
If you disagree with our shortlist or our findings, say so plainly and explain why.

research_request.output_format: 1. Executive summary (10 lines max): recommended tool + top 2 problem statements. 2. Tool comparison table, then the recommendation (T2). 3. Underwater assessment (T3). 4. Literature table grouped by theme (T1). 5. Refined problem statements (T4). 6. Stress-test and ranking table (T5). 7. Open questions for us to decide. 8. References in IEEE format with DOI or arXiv ID.
